author: William Saville
pairing: Aang / Katara / Toph Beifong / Jasper (consensual adult polycule)
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: The City from Above
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass three
content:
Appa did not approve of my map.

He made that clear by sneezing directly onto it.

The ink smudged across the east bank. I yelped, Aang laughed, and the enormous sky bison looked entirely satisfied with his contribution to urban planning.

"It's waterproof ink," Aang said.

"Apparently not bison-proof."

"Very little is."

I held the paper away from Appa's nose. The purpose of the flight was simple: survey the Riverstone floodplain from above, compare it with the older drainage diagram, and determine whether the recent bridge repairs had changed the way stormwater traveled. We had been asked to make observations. No one had asked us to solve an entire watershed before breakfast.

Aang had somehow brought enough food for a journey across three continents.

"Katara packed most of it before she left," he admitted as he adjusted the saddle.

That stopped me.

"She packed this?"

"She said I'd forget to eat while I was working."

"Accurate."

He smiled, but it didn't last.

We'd received one letter from the South. Katara was helping establish treatment rooms after a difficult storm season, and none of us knew when she'd be finished. The calendar we'd made before her departure was still on the kitchen wall, her planned evenings penciled in rather than crossed out.

I didn't want her absence turned into an emergency. I did want to hear her voice.

"Ready?" Aang asked.

I tucked the map into its case.

"Let's go."

Appa rose over Lanternwell Square with a slow, powerful motion that pulled my stomach toward my boots. The rooftops shrank beneath us. The seven districts took shape as actual places instead of a list of names: Tideglass Cove's bright water, Jasmine Steps curving around the garden, Brasswatch Yard with its straight workshop paths, Moonroot's dark roof, and the thin line of Starwake Pier reaching toward its own doorway.

From above, the Lanternweald looked small enough to cup in two hands.

It was not small enough to manage carelessly.

"Look at that," Aang said.

He pointed toward the spring below the well. Water had gathered behind a raised strip of earth, then diverted toward the gardens. A newer footpath crossed the old streambed at an angle.

"That's not on Fen's plan," I said.

"Or Neri's."

We landed in a clear meadow above Riverstone Terrace. I drew what we'd seen while Aang paced the path and tested the soil with gentle gusts of air. His bending could clear leaves from a blocked channel. It could reveal which stones were loose. It could not make a badly placed building disappear without deciding what would happen to the people inside it.

"Could you bend the water away?" I asked.

"Temporarily."

"And when you stop?"

"It finds its old route."

We stood in the grass for a long time.

Below us, a small market garden had been built on what appeared to be the natural spillway. The beds were productive. Someone had planted beans, herbs, and a row of purple flowers along the edges. Moving it would cost labor, food, and perhaps someone's only income.

Aang crouched beside the soil.

"I used to think if I could move the water, I'd fixed the problem," he said.

"Sometimes you have."

"Sometimes I've moved it into somebody else's home."

I marked the garden on the map.

"Then we ask the people who live there."

We followed the slope down to a house with blue shutters. A woman named Sela met us at the gate, wiping dirt from her hands. She had grown up tending the garden, and her grandmother had planted its first fruit tree.

"Floodwater used to run through here," she told us, "but the old stones kept it low. After the new path went in, it started collecting against the west wall."

Aang looked toward the path.

"Who approved it?"

"The neighborhood council. They needed a wider route for carts."

I felt a familiar irritation settle behind my ribs. Every improvement carried a cost; too often the cost was paid by someone who hadn't been at the meeting.

"Did they ask you?" I said.

"They showed us the plan after the work began."

Aang's expression changed.

He had helped design more than one public road. He knew what it felt like to be certain a plan was generous and discover that certainty had hidden an oversight.

"Would you be willing to meet with the survey group?" he asked.

Sela looked at him.

"Only if they're prepared to listen."

"I'll make sure they are."

"Don't make promises for other people," I murmured.

Aang caught himself.

"I'll ask them to listen," he corrected. "And I'll listen myself."

Sela nodded.

We spent the afternoon measuring the water marks along her wall. I wrote down the dates she remembered. Aang mapped the winds that carried heavy rain across the valley. We found that the new cart path had been laid on top of a narrow drainage cut, and that its packed gravel had blocked water moving toward the old service passage.

The seventh scratch beneath the well returned to my thoughts.

We were not ready to open anything. But we had enough evidence to stop treating the flood as a mysterious tantrum by the weather.

By the time Appa carried us home, the sky was pink.

Aang leaned beside me on the saddle, quiet.

"Do you miss her?" he asked.

"Every day."

"Me too."

He looked toward the South, though there was no way to see it from here.

"Sometimes when I'm away, I worry I'm the one being left behind."

I turned toward him.

"By Katara?"

"By all of us. The work keeps changing. The world keeps changing. I come home and I'm afraid the shape of our family will be different."

"It will be different."

He looked startled.

"That's supposed to comfort me?"

"Maybe not. But we're allowed to grow. The agreements we make aren't a spell keeping us frozen. We have to keep choosing them."

Aang considered that.

"What if we choose differently someday?"

"Then we tell the truth. We don't trap people with a promise they made before they knew what they needed."

He was quiet for a while.

Then he leaned close, brushing his forehead against mine.

"You're impossible."

"Toph says that."

"Toph says everyone is impossible."

"She has a point."

He kissed me gently, then grinned.

"Appa is watching."

"Appa sneezed on my map. He forfeited the right to judge."

When we landed, Toph was waiting with a bowl of dumplings and a list of questions.

"Well?" she demanded.

"We found the old spillway."

"Congratulations. Did the dirt look good from up there?"

"Very picturesque," I said.

"Did it tell you what happens underneath the path?"

"No."

She grinned.

"Then tomorrow we start with the ground."

We spread the stained map across the table. It smelled faintly of bison and evening air. Aang wrote Sela's name beside the garden, with a note that she needed to be present before anyone proposed moving it.

Katara's empty chair stood across from us.

I found myself smiling.

The survey had not fixed the floodplain. But we had stopped pretending the sky gave us every answer.
